transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-09
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Arjun Patel (Redwood SE), Nora Li (Redwood CSM), Lena Ortiz (Galactic Head of Platform), Tomás Rivera (Galactic SRE), Priya Shah (Galactic Security), Evan Cole (Galactic Product), Jada Kim (Galactic Oncall)

Summary: quick technical postmortem walkthrough from the surge event on 2026-07-03; handoff of mitigations, confirm telemetry gaps, agree pilot plan for dedicated capacity, and align on security/compliance artifacts for enterprise onboarding.

Topics: incident timeline, KV/prefix cache behavior, autoscale vs throttle tradeoffs, fallback routing and graceful degradation, security artifacts (KMS, SOC2), next steps for pilot and benchmarks.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we have about an hour, we'll run through the incident timeline, what we saw on our side, and then hand off the outstanding mitigations. arjun, you want to kick off with the quick timeline?
[00:18] Arjun Patel: yeah sure. so as a quick summary, at ~2026-07-03T22:14Z we saw a coordinated surge in request rate from galactic's primary region. throughput spiked, KV cache hit rate dropped from ~86% to 32% which exposed hot prefixes and caused token generation to queue up. the runtime started applying backpressure and then the throttle policy kicked in around t+4m which increased 429s for some customer routes.
[00:47] Tomás Rivera: yeah that matches our oncall alerts. the rate limiter alarms were the first thing that paged us. i think the confusing bit was the cache invalidation pattern — we had a batch job that rewrote many user keys and that coincided with the traffic spike.
[01:06] Arjun Patel: mhm, the combination was unfortunate. there was a cascade: cache miss ratio -> longer KV fetchs -> increased token latency -> request queueing -> autoscale couldn't keep up because of startup overhead for the chosen instance profile. so the SLO breach window was roughly 7 minutes.
[01:25] Lena Ortiz: quick q, when you say startup overhead, are we talking container cold start or GPU spin-up? in our telemetry it looked like gpus were idle but not accepting traffic for a bit.
[01:34] Arjun Patel: good question. it's mostly the model load and compilation path — the runtime chooses kernels and warms attention caches. sometimes we observe a 60-90s warmup on certain quantized build profiles. but in this case the bigger problem was a small fleet of instances that had been scaled down to zero per policy and required a scale-up.
[01:50] Jada Kim: there was also flapping in the canary config — the canary served two routes and we had a mismatch in model pinning, so fallback routing tried to redirect to a variant that had a different KV schema. that caused a bunch of errors too.
[02:05] Arjun Patel: yes, the fallback attempted to switch to a lighter quantized variant but it didn't share the same prefix layout so the cache key lookups failed. some of the error logs read like "key not found: prefix_v2" which is what jada mentioned.
[02:15] Nora Li: quick note — transcription might show this as 'kay vee' cache later, just fyi.
[02:19] (laughter)
[02:22] Priya Shah: from a security standpoint the big ask is we need to ensure any shared traces are sanitized. i'll only accept artifacts that have user ids redacted and customer tokens masked. and we need a KMS diagram before we hand off any keys.
[02:36] Maya Chen: absolutely. we'll give you sanitized traces; arjun will run an export and scrub PII. arjun, do you have an ETA?
[02:44] Arjun Patel: i'll aim for end of day monday — so 2026-07-13 — to upload annotated KV logs and a short writeup that highlights the cache churn and prefix changes.
[02:53] Evan Cole: on the product side, we want to understand what long-term controls we should use. do we lean into dedicated reserved capacity or tune hosted to be more conservative? there's a big price difference.
[03:06] Maya Chen: we discussed pricing scenarios in the pre-call doc. reserved capacity gives you predictable throughput — no cold starts in the same way — and we can carve an isolated GPU pool that matches your 99.9% tail. hosted with conservative autoscale and pre-warm policies could be cheaper if your traffic is spiky but predictable.
[03:22] Tomás Rivera: important to mention: our traffic is bursty — end-of-day settlement windows create 2x-5x bursts for 3-7 minutes. so the model needs that fast ramp.
[03:33] Arjun Patel: for that pattern we usually recommend a hybrid: a small reserved spine for baseline and burstable hosted slots for overflow. we can also pre-warm model instances by keeping a warm pool with minimal instance count so startup is negligible.
[03:46] Lena Ortiz: ok that sounds reasonable. what about software mitigations? you mentioned better fallback mapping and prefix compatibility.
[03:53] Arjun Patel: yeah, immediate fixes: 1) strict prefix compatibility checks during rollout — we can add a deployment hook to validate that model variants share cache schema; 2) turn on conservative throttle at 85% of concurrency so we avoid sudden 429 storms; 3) implement a short lived in-memory shadow KV for hot keys during cache rebuild.
[04:12] Tomás Rivera: shadow KV sounds interesting — is that managed by your runtime or do we have to implement in our service?
[04:18] Arjun Patel: managed by runtime — it's an ephemeral prefix cache that holds the last N keys for a route while the main cache is rebuilding. it reduces the miss storm. there are caveats — it increases memory and can harm cold path if misconfigured.
[04:30] Priya Shah: memory tradeoff is ok but we need to know the encryption posture for that shadow cache. does it use customer KMS keys when deployed in Private mode?
[04:38] Arjun Patel: in Private deployments it can be configured to use your KMS; in hosted we use our managed encryption and can support customer-managed keys in Dedicated depending on contract. we'll include that in the security doc.
[04:51] Maya Chen: quick interjection, we also detected a misconfigured autoscaling policy: the cooldown was 8m which is too long. we suggest reducing cooldown to 60-90s for these settlement windows.
[05:02] Jada Kim: noted. we can change cooldown but worried about oscillation — if we scale too fast we might thrash.
[05:10] Arjun Patel: that's why the pre-warm pool + conservative throttle + cooldown together give the best result. they smooth spikes without thrash.
[05:19] Lena Ortiz: can you show the specific log lines that indicate prefix mismatch — the ones that looked like 'prefix_v2' missing?
[05:26] Arjun Patel: sure, i'll paste examples in the postmortem doc. (typing) here's a snippet — "ERR cache lookup: prefix_v2::user:31293 not found" and then subsequent het calls to remote kv store. the latency climbs from ~30ms to 450ms on those paths.
[05:40] Tomás Rivera: one more operational ask — can we have a fail-open policy for non-critical routes so we don't block product flows during cache rebuilds?
[05:49] Arjun Patel: yes, we can set route-level degradations: degrade to best-effort sampling (lower token lengths), or fall back to a cheaper model variant where we accept slightly different output but preserve availability.
[05:58] Evan Cole: what's the expected delta in token costs if we route to the lighter variant during bursts?
[06:03] Maya Chen: typically 30-45% lower per-token cost for the quantized smaller variant, but quality differs. we'll share evals for the common prompt sets.
[06:12] Lena Ortiz: can we run a canary that verifies cache schema compatibility automatically?
[06:17] Arjun Patel: yes — we can block rollout if schema mismatch detected. it's a small CI check in the deployment pipeline. we can ship that into your canary fleet within 2 sprints — estimate 3 weeks — unless you want an expedited patch.
[06:29] Priya Shah: security question — you said dedicated supports CMKs. do you support HSM-backed keys? our compliance needs that for later stages.
[06:37] Arjun Patel: HSM-backed Cloud KMS is supported in Dedicated and Private. we'll need to work through the KMS ACLs and rotation window, and document it in the enterprise readiness checklist.
[06:49] Nora Li: i'm going to flag a telemetry gap — during the surge a couple of internal metrics dropped out (sampling agent OOM) so we lost ~90s of traces. arjun, is that something you can still reconstruct?
[06:58] Arjun Patel: partially. we have aggregate metrics from the serving plane and some event logs from the routing layer. we lack high-fidelity per-request traces for that 90s, which is why we asked for galactic's local logs.
[07:08] Jada Kim: we'll provide sanitized request logs from our side, but we need a template for what fields you need.
[07:14] Maya Chen: i'll share the template after the call. arjun, should include timestamp, route, model_variant, cache_hit, latency_ms, and error_code fields.
[07:24] (crosstalk)
[07:26] Tomás Rivera: ok i want to raise a procurement-ish item — if we go with dedicated reserved capacity, what's the shortest contract? we want Q3 pilot before committing to year-long.
[07:36] Maya Chen: we can do monthly reserved pilot for 3 months — it's a shorter-term reserved allocation. pricing will be prorated. i'll include a couple scenarios in the follow-up.
[07:46] Evan Cole: and the SLA for that pilot — do you offer an SLO-backed credit?
[07:51] Maya Chen: yes, for dedicated we can extend an SLA-backed credit structure. terms will need legal review.
[07:57] Priya Shah: one more security checklist item: audit logs retention, RBAC, and SSO. we need to map to our internal policies and determine if additional admin roles are needed.
[08:08] Arjun Patel: audit logs: in Dedicated we can push logs to your logging endpoint, set retention per policy, and we support SAML SSO + SCIM for user provisioning.
[08:19] Lena Ortiz: what's the typical retention windows you support?
[08:22] Arjun Patel: default is 90 days in-hosted, but for enterprise/dedicated we can do custom retention: 1 year, 2 years, etc., depending on storage. we'll include options in the security packet.
[08:33] (brief pause)
[08:36] Nora Li: okay let's pivot to immediate mitigations and timeline. arjun, walk me through the 0-30 day plan.
[08:43] Arjun Patel: immediate (0-7 days): scrub and share traces, reduce autoscale cooldown to 90s, enable conservative route throttle at 85% concurrency, and deploy a hot-key shadow cache. short term (7-30 days): implement prefix-compatibility CI hook, add warm-pool policy for settlement windows, run a controlled chaos test to validate fallback behavior. medium term (30-90 days): pilot dedicated reserved spine, integrate CMK/HSM keys, and expand telemetry to remove sampling blindspots.
[09:13] Jada Kim: chaos testing — we want to run a drumbeat during pre-prod to simulate the exact settlement pattern. can redwood assist?
[09:20] Arjun Patel: yes we can provide a scripted load harness and a test plan; we'll run it jointly with your SREs.
[09:26] Lena Ortiz: that would be great. also can you include a runbook tweak that specifies who will be paged and what thresholds trigger a rollback? last incident had a lot of decision latency.
[09:36] Maya Chen: we'll revise the runbook. nora, can you own updating the runbook docs?
[09:41] Nora Li: yes, i'll update the runbook and share for review by 2026-07-15.
[09:46] Tomás Rivera: regarding rollback — do you support blue/green or immediate rollback for model variants?
[09:51] Arjun Patel: both. we support canary and blue/green. rollback is automated if health checks fail the canary; for some deployments we support automatic fallback to a pinned variant.
[09:59] Evan Cole: can we add a metric for user-facing errors per minute as a canary gate?
[10:03] Arjun Patel: yes, we can add user_error_rate and tail_latency as rollout gates.
[10:08] Priya Shah: small nit — make sure the SOC2 artifact we exchange includes the subservice provider list. we can't accept black boxes without that.
[10:16] Maya Chen: noted — i'll include ssp list in the security packet.
[10:20] Lena Ortiz: let's capture explicit acceptance criteria for the pilot: 1) 99.9% availability during 5-minute settlement bursts over a 2-week window, 2) no more than 0.5% error rate regression, 3) agreed price delta for overflow capacity.
[10:36] Maya Chen: sounds good. i'll draft the pilot success criteria and circulate.
[10:40] (typing noises)
[10:42] Arjun Patel: quick clarification on the cache shadow: default memory budget is configurable per route — recommend starting with 200MB for the settlement flows and adjusting from there.
[10:53] Tomás Rivera: we'll start with that and report impact.
[10:56] Jada Kim: regarding the missing traces, we'll attach our local ingress logs. what's the preferred format?
[11:02] Maya Chen: JSON lines with fields we listed earlier is best. please gzip and upload to the shared drive.
[11:08] Priya Shah: any redwood internal action on encryption we should be aware of?
[11:12] Arjun Patel: we'll document encryption-in-transit, at-rest specifics and CMK flows. for HSM-backed keys we may need an additional joint work session.
[11:21] Lena Ortiz: last question — how quickly can you turn on the prefix-compatibility CI gate? expedited patch?
[11:27] Arjun Patel: we can fast-track a minimal validation in 5 business days if your team wants to prioritize; full integration into the pipeline will take longer.
[11:35] Maya Chen: OK let's get a quick decision from galactic — do you want the expedited gate?
[11:40] Lena Ortiz: yes, expedite please. we'll mark it as priority.
[11:44] (short pause)
[11:46] Maya Chen: cool. to wrap up, recap of commitments: arjun uploads sanitized KV/prefix traces by 2026-07-13; nora updates runbook by 2026-07-15; maya sends pilot draft and pricing by 2026-07-14; priya and lena exchange SOC2/KMS artifact list by 2026-07-16; schedule load test week of 2026-07-20.
[12:07] Tomás Rivera: thanks everyone, appreciate the quick coordination.
[12:11] Maya Chen: thanks, we'll follow up with a calendar invite for the load test and a shared drive link for artifacts.
[12:17] (meeting ends)
